text: Wi-Fi security has gone through three real generations. WEP, the original standard, has been considered broken since the early 2000s. WPA2, using AES encryption and a four-way handshake, is still the most common standard in use today. WPA3 is the current standard, and an analyst needs to recognize all three on sight, not just assume the newest one is everywhere.

When a device joins a WPA2 network, it derives a shared key from the password and the network name, then exchanges four messages with the access point to confirm both sides hold the same session key — without ever sending that key itself over the air. That handshake is also WPA2's best-known weakness: an attacker who captures it can attempt an offline dictionary attack against the password.

That's exactly what WPA3 fixes. It replaces the password exchange with SAE, sometimes called the dragonfly handshake, which resists the offline dictionary attacks that work against a captured WPA2 handshake. WPA3 also adds forward secrecy, so a later password leak can't retroactively decrypt earlier captured traffic, and it encrypts even open-network traffic that previously had none.

Open Wi-Fi, the kind with no password, has no encryption between the device and the access point at all. HTTPS still protects an individual connection's content, but the network itself offers no protection, which is exactly the environment the next attack depends on.

A rogue access point is any unauthorized Wi-Fi access point near a network. An evil twin is the common version: an attacker broadcasts the same network name as a legitimate hotspot, hoping a device connects to the fake one instead. Once that happens, the attacker sits in the middle of the traffic, able to observe it, redirect to fake login pages, or inject malicious content.

It works because most people have no reliable way to tell two identically named networks apart. That closes out ports, protocols, and network services.
